lead: The CMOS inverter is one nMOS pull-down and one pMOS pull-up. Its voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) plots Vout against Vin at a fixed supply VDD. The curve sets the switching threshold VM, the output high and low levels VOH and VOL, and the noise margins NMH and NML. These numbers tell a designer whether a gate will restore a weak logic level and how much noise an input can take. The same curve is the first check on every standard cell, memory bit cell and level shifter.
prereq: You need: MOS operating regions and drain-current equations from Unit 1, and the CMOS cross-section from Unit 2; the load comparison appears in Chapter 3.2.

sections.h3: The five regions of the VTC

blocks.text: The CMOS inverter has an nMOS pull-down and a pMOS pull-up. The voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) plots V<sub>out</sub> against V<sub>in</sub> at a fixed supply V<sub>DD</sub>. V<sub>OH</sub> is the high output, V<sub>OL</sub> the low output, and V<sub>M</sub> the input where V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub>. V<sub>tn</sub> and |V<sub>tp</sub>| are the nMOS and pMOS threshold magnitudes.

The five regions follow from the transistor states. (1) V<sub>in</sub> < V<sub>tn</sub>: nMOS off, pMOS linear, V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>. (2) V<sub>tn</sub> ≤ V<sub>in</sub> < V<sub>M</sub>: nMOS saturation, pMOS linear; V<sub>out</sub> falls. (3) V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>M</sub>: both transistors in saturation. (4) V<sub>M</sub> < V<sub>in</sub> ≤ V<sub>DD</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|: nMOS linear, pMOS saturation; V<sub>out</sub> approaches 0 V. (5) V<sub>in</sub> > V<sub>DD</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|: pMOS off, nMOS linear, V<sub>out</sub> = 0 V.

Each region comes from Kirchhoff's current law at the output: the nMOS drain current equals the pMOS drain current. I<sub>D</sub> is drain current, V<sub>GS</sub> is gate-source voltage and V<sub>DS</sub> is drain-source voltage. In saturation I<sub>D</sub> = (β/2)(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>t</sub>)²; in linear I<sub>D</sub> = β[(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>t</sub>)V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>²/2].

blocks.where: β is the transconductance parameter in A/V²; μ is carrier mobility; C<sub>ox</sub> is oxide capacitance per area; W/L is the width-to-length ratio.

blocks.text: At V<sub>M</sub> set β<sub>n</sub>(V<sub>M</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>)² = β<sub>p</sub>(V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>M</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|)². Taking positive square roots gives the design equation.

blocks.where: V<sub>M</sub> is the switching threshold in volts; r is the strength ratio, dimensionless; V<sub>DD</sub>, V<sub>tn</sub> and |V<sub>tp</sub>| are in volts.

sections.h3: Noise margins and the matched case

blocks.text: V<sub>IL</sub> is the largest input still treated as low; V<sub>IH</sub> is the smallest input still treated as high. They are the points where the VTC slope dV<sub>out</sub>/dV<sub>in</sub> = −1. The noise margins are the gaps between the guaranteed output levels and these input limits.
NM<sub>H</sub> = V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>IH</sub>, NM<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>
blocks.where: NM<sub>H</sub> is the high noise margin and NM<sub>L</sub> is the low noise margin, both in volts; V<sub>OH</sub> and V<sub>OL</sub> are the output high and low levels.

blocks.text: A matched inverter has β<sub>n</sub> = β<sub>p</sub> and V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>|. Then r = 1 and V<sub>M</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>/2. For V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V, V<sub>M</sub> = 2.5 V. The figure uses these values.

Read V<sub>OH</sub> and V<sub>OL</sub> from the flat parts: V<sub>OH</sub> = 5 V and V<sub>OL</sub> = 0 V in the ideal curve. A larger β<sub>n</sub>/β<sub>p</sub> makes r larger and pulls V<sub>M</sub> down; a stronger pMOS pulls it up.
With V<sub>M</sub> away from V<sub>DD</sub>/2, one noise margin shrinks before the other. That is why symmetric sizing is common in gates that must accept signals from both directions.

The pMOS overdrive is V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>in</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|, because the pMOS source is at V<sub>DD</sub>. The nMOS overdrive is V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>. Mixing these expressions is a common sign error.

Use the VTC to check a chain: each gate must drive the next gate so that its output high is at least VIH and its output low is at most VIL, both by the required margin. After DC design, the same widths set load capacitance and delay; see Chapter 3.3. Power follows in Chapter 3.5.

Some syllabi call this the DC transfer characteristic; for a memory cell drawn in both directions it is the butterfly curve. The static CMOS gate in Chapter 3.7 repeats this inverter as its output stage.

For the figure, V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.6 V, |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V and β<sub>n</sub> = β<sub>p</sub>. Then V<sub>M</sub> = (5 + 0.6 − 0.6)/2 = 2.5 V. The plotted crossing at (2.5 V, 2.5 V) is V<sub>M</sub>.

figure.caption: Voltage transfer curve for a matched inverter with VDD = 5 V and Vtn = |Vtp| = 0.6 V. The crossing at 2.5 V is VM; the flat rails show the restored high and low levels.

spec.aria: A voltage transfer curve that stays high, falls steeply through the middle, and stays low.

examples.question: A matched CMOS inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 3.3 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.6 V, |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V and β<sub>n</sub> = β<sub>p</sub>. Find V<sub>M</sub>, and state the region of both transistors at V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>M</sub>. Also find each overdrive voltage.
steps: At V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>M</sub>, both transistors are in saturation. Equate saturation currents: β<sub>n</sub>(V<sub>M</sub> − 0.6)² = β<sub>p</sub>(3.3 − V<sub>M</sub> − 0.6)².
Equal β gives V<sub>M</sub> − 0.6 = 3.3 − V<sub>M</sub> − 0.6 = 2.7 − V<sub>M</sub>. Thus 2V<sub>M</sub> = 3.3 V, so V<sub>M</sub> = 1.65 V.
At V<sub>M</sub>, V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>M</sub> = 1.65 V. nMOS: V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.65 V, V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.65 V, overdrive = 1.65 − 0.6 = 1.05 V. V<sub>DS</sub> > overdrive, so saturation.
pMOS: V<sub>SG</sub> = 3.3 − 1.65 = 1.65 V, |V<sub>SD</sub>| = 3.3 − 1.65 = 1.65 V, overdrive = 1.65 − 0.6 = 1.05 V. |V<sub>SD</sub>| > overdrive, so saturation.
examples.answer: V<sub>M</sub> = 1.65 V; both transistors are in saturation with overdrive 1.05 V each.
examples.check:
vdd = 3.3
vtn = 0.6
vtp = 0.6
vm = (vdd + vtn - vtp) / 2
ov_n = vm - vtn
ov_p = vdd - vm - vtp
print(round(vm, 2))
print(round(ov_n, 2))
print(round(ov_p, 2))

traps: Do not assume V<sub>M</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>/2 unless β<sub>n</sub> = β<sub>p</sub> and V<sub>tn</sub> = |V<sub>tp</sub>|; a stronger nMOS lowers V<sub>M</sub>.
The pMOS overdrive is V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>in</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|, not V<sub>in</sub> − |V<sub>tp</sub>|; the pMOS source sits at V<sub>DD</sub>.
V<sub>IL</sub> and V<sub>IH</sub> are not the transistor threshold voltages; they are the input points where |dV<sub>out</sub>/dV<sub>in</sub>| = 1.

Noise margin is not the same as logic swing; swing is V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>, while NM<sub>H</sub> = V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>IH</sub> and NM<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub> subtract the undefined input bands.

quiz.q: Define V<sub>M</sub>, V<sub>OH</sub> and V<sub>OL</sub> for a CMOS inverter.
quiz.a: V<sub>M</sub> is the input voltage where V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub>. V<sub>OH</sub> is the output high level and V<sub>OL</sub> is the output low level.

quiz.q: Why are V<sub>OH</sub> and V<sub>OL</sub> close to the supply rails in an ideal CMOS inverter?
quiz.a: When one transistor is off, the other is on and connects the output to its rail, so the output reaches V<sub>DD</sub> or 0 V. Because the off transistor breaks the supply-to-ground path, no steady current flows and the levels stay at the rails.

quiz.q: A matched inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.6 V and |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V. Find V<sub>M</sub>.
quiz.a: Matched gives r = 1. V<sub>M</sub> = (5 + 0.6 − 0.6)/2 = 2.5 V. Both devices are in saturation at this point.

quiz.q: An inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.6 V, |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V and β<sub>n</sub> = 4β<sub>p</sub>. Find V<sub>M</sub>.
A designer doubles β<sub>n</sub> in an otherwise matched inverter. How does V<sub>M</sub> move, and which noise margin tends to shrink?
quiz.a: V<sub>M</sub> moves down because the nMOS is stronger. The curve shifts left, so NM<sub>H</sub> tends to rise and NM<sub>L</sub> tends to shrink.

quiz.q: Why is V<sub>IL</sub> not simply equal to V<sub>tn</sub>?
quiz.a: V<sub>IL</sub> is defined by the VTC slope reaching −1, not by the device turning on. It depends on both transistor currents and sizes, so it differs from V<sub>tn</sub>.

quiz.q: At V<sub>in</sub> = 2 V in a 3.3 V matched inverter with V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.6 V and |V<sub>tp</sub>| = 0.6 V, find both overdrives.
quiz.a: nMOS overdrive = 2 − 0.6 = 1.4 V. pMOS overdrive = 3.3 − 2 − 0.6 = 0.7 V. The nMOS is stronger at this input.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the VTC is generated by SPICE across process, voltage and temperature corners before a standard cell is released. The same curve, drawn for both inverters of a six-transistor SRAM cell, gives the static noise margin called the butterfly curve. FinFET and low-voltage designs make the near-threshold VTC less steep, so read noise margin at the actual supply. Search next for static noise margin, SPICE DC sweep and process corners.
